books.section: Topic 4.8 Jackson and Federal Power, B. Contention Between Whites and American Indians over Western Lands
The Jackson Presidency and Jacksonian Democracy

stimulus.text: The portrait, published in 1838, shows Sequoyah (Se-Quo-Yah), a Cherokee leader, holding a tablet covered with the characters of the Cherokee syllabary, the writing system he invented. The Cherokee used the syllabary to print their own newspaper, the Cherokee Phoenix, beginning in 1828.
stimulus.source_note: Portrait 'Se-Quo-Yah,' McKenney-Hall series, drawn, printed and coloured at I. T. Bowen's Lithographic Establishment, Philadelphia, published 1838 (Library of Congress). Public domain; image viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: In Worcester v. Georgia (1832), the Supreme Court ruled that Georgia's laws had no force in Cherokee territory. Why did the ruling not stop removal?

options.text: The Supreme Court reversed itself the next year
options.misconception: A ruling that changed nothing invites the thought that the Court itself took it back.

options.text: The Cherokee agreed to leave immediately
options.misconception: A treaty exists, so it is easy to think the whole nation agreed to leave.

options.text: Jackson refused to enforce the ruling
Congress repealed the Indian Removal Act
options.misconception: A law that failed invites the thought that Congress repealed it.

rationales.A: The Court never reversed Worcester; the ruling stood, but no one in power enforced it.
rationales.B: Most Cherokee, led by John Ross, resisted removal for years; only a small minority signed the Treaty of New Echota in 1835.
rationales.C: Jackson sided with Georgia and did not enforce the Court's decision, so Georgia kept pressing removal and federal troops later carried it out.
rationales.D: Congress never repealed the Removal Act of 1830; the law stayed on the books while removal went ahead.
rationales.general:
1. Read the ruling. Worcester said the Cherokee were a distinct community where Georgia's laws had no force.
2. Ask who enforces a ruling. Courts decide; presidents enforce, and Jackson, who backed Georgia, did not act.
Background: Georgia pressed on, and in 1838 federal troops forced the Cherokee west on the Trail of Tears.
Remember: a court ruling is only as strong as the enforcement behind it — ask who was supposed to enforce it.
